sections.8-7: Given Objective and Constraints: Solve Completely

bank.q: Linear programming is...
bank.a: A model of linear relationships representing a firm's objective and resource constraints
d: A method for writing computer programs in a straight line
A model of curved relationships between profit and time
A statistical test for comparing two means
bank.why: Slide 2: LP is a model consisting of linear relationships representing a firm's objective and resource constraints.
bank.hint: Linear + objective + constraints.

bank.q: In an LP problem, the quantity that must be maximized or minimized is the...
bank.why: The objective function (e.g. $P = 30x + 40y$) is what you maximize or minimize.
bank.hint: Your goal.

bank.q: Inequalities or equations that restrict the values of the variables are called...
bank.why: The objective function is subject to constraints.
bank.hint: They restrict.

bank.q: LP is used to find...
bank.a: The best (optimal) way to use limited resources to reach a goal
d: The average of a set of data
The slope of a single straight line
Every possible solution, not just the best one
bank.why: Slide 2: the best or optimal solution for using limited resources.
bank.hint: Optimal.

bank.q: In the LP model, $x_j$ stands for the...
bank.why: $x_j$ = decision variables; $b_i$ = constraint levels; $c_j$ = objective function coefficients; $a_{ij}$ = constraint coefficients.
bank.hint: What you decide.

bank.q: In the LP model, $b_i$ stands for the...
bank.why: $b_i$ is the right-hand side of each constraint: the limit (e.g. 32 labor-hours).
bank.hint: The right-hand side.

bank.q: In $z = c_1x_1 + c_2x_2 + \dots + c_nx_n$, the $c_j$ are the...
bank.why: $c_j$ multiplies each variable in the objective function (e.g. the ₱500 and ₱800 profits).
bank.hint: In z.

bank.q: In the constraint $a_{11}x_1 + a_{12}x_2 \le b_1$, the $a_{ij}$ are the...
bank.why: $a_{ij}$ are the coefficients inside the constraints (e.g. 1 and 2 labor-hours).
bank.hint: Inside the constraints.

bank.q: In the model Max $P = 500x + 800y$ subject to $x + 2y \le 32$, $3x + 4y \le 84$, $x, y \ge 0$, what is 84?
bank.why: 84 is the maximum labor-hours of the assembly department: the right-hand side.
bank.hint: Right-hand side.

bank.q: In Max $P = 500x + 800y$, what are 500 and 800?
bank.why: They are the $c_j$: the profit each unit adds to P.
bank.hint: In the objective.

bank.q: What are the two approaches to linear programming?
bank.why: Slide 4: geometric → graphical; algebraic → simplex.
bank.hint: Graph vs algebra.

bank.q: The simplex method was developed by...
bank.why: Slide 4: George B. Dantzig, 1947.
bank.hint: Dantzig.

bank.q: When is the simplex (algebraic) method used instead of the graphical method?
bank.a: When there are more decision variables and constraints
d: When there are exactly two variables
When the problem has no constraints
When the answer must be a fraction
bank.why: Graphs work for two variables; simplex handles more.
bank.hint: Too many to graph.

bank.q: The graphical method finds the optimal solution using...
bank.a: The feasible region and its corner points
d: The slope of the objective only
bank.why: Slide 4: feasible region and corner (coordinate) points.
bank.hint: Shade, then check corners.

bank.q: What is the order of the steps in formulating an LP model?
bank.a: Read and tabulate → define variables → objective function → constraints → solve
d: Define variables → solve → constraints → objective → read
Objective → read → constraints → solve → define variables
Constraints → objective → define variables → read → solve
bank.why: Slide 8: 1 read (table), 2 variables, 3 objective function, 4 constraint inequalities, 5 solve.
bank.hint: Read first, solve last.

bank.q: "Determine and define the variables" is which step?
bank.why: 1 read, 2 variables, 3 objective, 4 constraints, 5 solve.
bank.hint: After reading.

bank.q: Why do production problems include $x \ge 0$ and $y \ge 0$?
bank.a: You cannot produce a negative quantity
d: They make the objective function larger
They are needed only in minimization
bank.why: Slide 13: non-negativity constraints.
bank.hint: No negative tents.

bank.q: The optimal solution of an LP problem is most likely at a corner point (vertex) of the feasible region.
bank.why: Slide 15: corner points most likely carry the optimal solution.

bank.q: The feasible region is the shaded area bounded by the constraint lines.
bank.why: Slide 15.

bank.hint: Intersect the boundary lines (including the axes) and keep only points that satisfy every constraint.

bank.q: For Minimize $C = 5x + 2y$ subject to $x + 3y \ge 12$, $x + y \ge 8$, $x, y \ge 0$, why can we find a MINIMUM but not a MAXIMUM?
bank.a: The feasible region is unbounded (it extends without end), so C can grow without limit
d: The region is empty, so no solution exists
Both constraints are ≤, so the region is closed
Minimum and maximum are always at the same corner
bank.why: With ≥ constraints the region opens upward and to the right; C has a smallest value (16 at (0, 8)) but no largest.
bank.hint: Look at the shaded region.

bank.q: Which inequality is the cutting-department constraint?
bank.why: Standard: 1 h, expedition: 2 h, at most 32 h a day.
bank.hint: 1 h and 2 h, at most 32.

bank.q: Which inequality is the assembly-department constraint?
bank.why: Standard: 3 h, expedition: 4 h, at most 84 h a day.
bank.hint: 3 h and 4 h, at most 84.

bank.q: Why are the tent constraints written with $\le$?
bank.a: The hours used cannot exceed the maximum labor-hours available
d: The company wants at least that many hours
bank.why: "Maximum labor-hours" → at most → $\le$.
bank.hint: Maximum available.

bank.q: In the diet problem, let $x$ = cups of drink X and $y$ = cups of drink Y. Which is the objective?
bank.why: Costs: $\$0.12$ per cup of X and $\$0.15$ per cup of Y; we want the lowest cost.
bank.hint: Cost, minimized.

bank.q: Which constraint says the drinks give at least 300 calories?
bank.why: Both drinks give 60 calories per cup; "at least" → $\ge$.
bank.hint: At least → ≥.

bank.q: Which constraint is for vitamin A (at least 36 units)?
bank.why: X gives 12 units, Y gives 6 units of vitamin A.
bank.hint: 12 and 6.

bank.q: Which constraint is for vitamin C (at least 90 units)?
bank.why: X gives 10 units, Y gives 30 units of vitamin C.

bank.q: In word problems, "at least" becomes ___ and "at most / maximum available" becomes ___.
bank.why: Requirements (at least) → ≥; limited resources (at most) → ≤.
bank.hint: Least → ≥.

bank.q: Why organize a word problem's data into a table first (Step 1)?

d: To find the corner points without graphing
To decide whether to maximize or minimize randomly
bank.why: The table rows become the constraints; the profit/cost row becomes the objective.
bank.hint: Rows → constraints.

bank.q: Ashlea runs a home bakery. A batch of ensaymada needs 1 hour of prep and 2 hours of oven time and earns ₱50 profit. A tray of pandesal needs 1 hour of prep and 1 hour of oven time and earns ₱40. Each day she has at most 10 hours of prep time and 16 hours of oven time. How many batches of ensaymada and trays of pandesal give the greatest daily profit? What is that profit?
bank.a: 6 batches of ensaymada and 4 trays of pandesal, for a maximum daily profit of ₱460

notes: Linear programming — a model of linear relationships for a firm's objective and resource constraints | Objective function — the function to maximize or minimize, $z = c_1x_1 + \dots + c_nx_n$ | Constraints — inequalities/equations that restrict the variables | Goal — the optimal use of limited resources
$x_j$ — decision variables | $b_i$ — constraint levels (right-hand sides) | $c_j$ — objective function coefficients | $a_{ij}$ — constraint coefficients
Geometric — graphical method: feasible region + corner points (2 variables) | Algebraic — simplex method, George B. Dantzig (1947): many variables and constraints

1 — graph each constraint as a line (find its x- and y-intercepts) | 2 — shade the side that satisfies it ($\le$: usually toward the origin; test (0, 0)) | 3 — feasible region = where all shadings overlap (with $x, y \ge 0$) | 4 — corner points = intersections of boundary lines | 5 — evaluate the objective at every corner; max or min wins | 6 — state the decision

Step 1 — read; organize the data in a table | Step 2 — define the variables | Step 3 — objective function (max or min) | Step 4 — constraint inequalities (+ non-negativity) | Step 5 — solve (graphically or with software)
At least, minimum required — $\ge$ | At most, maximum available, no more than — $\le$ | Profit, revenue — maximize | Cost — minimize | Can't produce negative amounts — $x, y \ge 0$

1 — make a table: one row per resource or requirement, one column per product | 2 — let $x$ and $y$ be the quantities you decide | 3 — profit → max, cost → min | 4 — available / at most → $\le$, needed / at least → $\ge$, plus $x, y \ge 0$ | 5 — intercepts of each line, shade, find every corner (solve two lines together for inside corners) | 6 — plug every corner into the objective | 7 — write the decision in words with units and pesos

Example 1 — max $P = 190$ at $(1, 4)$ | Example 2 — max $P = 28$ at $(2, 4)$ | Example 3 — min $C = 16$ at $(0, 8)$; unbounded, no max | Tents — max $P = ₱14{,}800$ at $(20, 6)$: 20 standard, 6 expedition | Diet — min $C = \$0.66$ at $(3, 2)$: 3 cups X, 2 cups Y
